prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My heart is a-breaking, dear Tittie, Some counsel unto me come len'; To anger them a' is a pity, But what will I do wi' Tam Glen? I'm thinking, wi' sic a braw fellow, In poortith I might mak a fen': What care I in riches to wallow, If I mauna marry Tam Glen? There's Lowrie, the laird o' Dumeller, "Guid-day to you,"—brute! he comes ben: He brags and he blaws o' his siller, But when will he dance like Tam Glen? My minnie does constantly deave me, And bids me beware o' young men; They flatter, she says, to deceive me; But wha can think sae o' Tam Glen? My daddie says, gin I'll forsake him, He'll gie me guid hunder marks ten: But, if it's ordain'd I maun take him, O wha will I get but Tam Glen? Yestreen at the valentines' dealing, My heart to my mou gied a sten: For thrice I drew ane without failing, And thrice it was written, "Tam Glen"! The last Halloween I was waukin My droukit sark-sleeve, as ye ken: His likeness cam up the house staukin, And the very gray breeks o' Tam Glen! Come counsel, dear Tittie, don't tarry; I'll gie ye my bonie black hen, Gif ye will advise me to marry The lad I lo'e dearly, Tam Glen.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Tittie, Some, But

outputs.L1:
My heart is breaking, dear Tittie;  
Come, lend me some counsel, I pray.  
It would be a pity to anger them all,  
Yet what am I to do about Tam Glen?

I think that, with such a fine fellow,  
Even in poverty I might manage well.  
What care I for wallowing in riches,  
If I may not marry Tam Glen?

There is Lowrie, the laird of Dumeller—  
“Good day to you”—the brute comes in.  
He boasts and blusters of his silver,  
But when will he dance like Tam Glen?

My mother constantly wearies me,  
And bids me beware of young men.  
They flatter, she says, only to deceive me;  
But who could think so of Tam Glen?

My father says that, if I forsake him,  
He will give me a good ten hundred marks.  
But if it is ordained that I must take someone,  
Oh, whom shall I have but Tam Glen?

Last night, at the drawing of valentines,  
My heart leapt into my mouth;  
For three times I drew one, without fail,  
And three times it was written: “Tam Glen.”

Last Halloween, as I was watching  
My drenched shirt-sleeve, as you know,  
His likeness came striding through the house—  
And even the very grey breeches of Tam Glen!

Come, counsel me, dear Tittie; do not delay.  
I will give you my bonny black hen  
If you will advise me to marry  
The lad I dearly love—Tam Glen.
outputs.L2:
My heart is breaking, dear Tittie;  
come and lend me some advice.  
It would be a shame to make them all angry,  
but what am I to do about Tam Glen?

I keep thinking that, with such a fine young man,  
I could manage even in poverty.  
Why should I care about living among riches  
if I am not allowed to marry Tam Glen?

There is Lowrie, the laird of Dumeller—  
“Good day to you,” says the brute as he comes in.  
He boasts and blusters about his money,  
but when could he ever dance like Tam Glen?

My mother never stops troubling me,  
warning me to be cautious of young men.  
She says they use sweet words only to trick me,  
but who could believe that of Tam Glen?

My father says that if I give him up,  
he will give me a good eleven hundred marks.  
But if it is my fate that I must choose someone,  
who else could I choose except Tam Glen?

Last night, when the valentines were being drawn,  
my heart leapt right up to my mouth.  
Three times I drew one, without mistake,  
and three times the name written there was “Tam Glen.”

Last Halloween, while I was watching  
my soaked shirt-sleeve, as you know,  
his image came striding into the house—  
even wearing the very gray breeches of Tam Glen.

So come give me counsel, dear Tittie; do not delay.  
I will give you my pretty black hen  
if only you advise me to marry  
the lad I love so dearly, Tam Glen.
outputs.L3:
The speaker confides in her dear friend Tittie, asking for advice because she is deeply troubled over whether she should marry Tam Glen. She is anxious and uncertain, not because she doubts her affection for him, but because others around her question the wisdom of the match. In her distress, she turns to Tittie as someone she trusts, hoping for sympathy and guidance.

What matters most to the speaker is Tam Glen himself—his character, his charm, and the happiness she believes he would bring her. She does not judge him by his wealth or social position. In fact, she suggests that poverty would be easier to bear if she could share her life with him. To her, love and companionship are far more valuable than money, and she would rather live modestly with Tam Glen than enjoy comfort with a man she does not love.

Other suitors are available to her, including the wealthy Lowrie, but they do not interest her. Lowrie may have money and security to offer, yet he cannot compete with Tam Glen in her eyes. No matter how respectable or prosperous these other men may be, they lack the qualities that have won her heart. For the speaker, Tam Glen stands apart from all the rest.

Her parents, however, strongly discourage her attachment. They warn her about young men and try to persuade her to give Tam Glen up. They even offer her money if she will forsake him, hoping that practical advantage will outweigh her feelings. But their efforts fail. The speaker remains loyal and devoted, showing that her love for Tam Glen is not easily shaken by pressure, warnings, or promises of financial reward.

She also finds reassurance in omens and traditional customs. Signs connected with valentines and Halloween seem to point toward Tam Glen as her destined husband. These customs strengthen her belief that her love is not merely a passing fancy, but something confirmed by fate. In the end, the speaker presents herself as a young woman torn by outside opposition, yet inwardly convinced that Tam Glen is the man she is meant to marry.
outputs.L4:
The speaker addresses her intimate friend, “dear Tittie,” and opens her heart about the question that is troubling her: should she marry Tam Glen? Everyone around her seems to have an opinion. Her family pressures her to choose a more respectable or wealthier match, and other suitors may be able to offer money, property, and social approval. Yet none of these advantages can quiet her feelings, because her heart is already drawn toward Tam.

As she reflects, the speaker weighs worldly concerns against affection. She knows that parents often value security and status, and she understands that a rich husband might seem like the wiser choice. Still, wealth cannot create love, and obedience to family wishes cannot replace genuine happiness. She turns instead to the signs and customs associated with love, reading omens and folk beliefs as confirmations of what she already feels. These signs all seem to point in the same direction: Tam Glen is the one meant for her.

By the end, the speaker’s uncertainty gives way to conviction. She recognizes that love is worth more than money, rank, or parental approval. Though others may advise her to choose a richer or more socially acceptable husband, her own heart and the traditional signs of love agree. She therefore affirms her devotion to Tam Glen, concluding that true affection is the strongest guide in marriage.
outputs.L5: Tittie was the name of a tiny, cheerful bird that lived near the edge of a quiet forest. Some mornings, it would sing from the highest branch, filling the air with bright, happy notes. But when storms arrived, Tittie would hide safely among the leaves, waiting patiently for the sky to clear. Its simple life reminded everyone nearby that even the smallest creatures can bring joy to the world.
